Based on the recommendations of this article: THE EFFECT OF EXTERNAL INTERFERENCE ON AVALANCHE TRANSCEIVER FUNCTIONALITY

Based on the results of this study, it is recommended that all electronic devices be turned off while attempting to search with an avalanche transceiver. This includes electronic devices that were not tested in this study. If items must remain on during a search, then the searching beacon should be held more than 40cm away from that object. As a broader rule, having all electronic devices, besides for avalanche transceivers, turned off while traveling in avalanche terrain is recommended, especially in this era of increasing technological use.

For more sources, see HERE: The avalanche review, and HERE: Wildsnow's own electronic interference testing
Reminder: Turn off all electronic devices while searching with an avalanche tranceiver!

Have you done much testing? My ski buddies and I have went to a city park awhile back to do some hooded training. Just trying to identify people's locations without looking up.

We also tested the cell phone theory and found it to be true. We used a Tracker 1, 2 and a 3 and found that the Tracker 1 was most interrupted by a cell phone in close proximity and only an issue while searching. We didn't see a lot of issues using a Tracker 2 or Tracker 3 to identify a Tracker 1 with a cell phone literally back to back with the transceiver. Overall we did see where having a cell phone turned on and near a transceiver was a bad idea for accuracy, but it didn't stop someone from finding people. In the heat of the moment, if you are searching for someone and you have a cell phone turned on in your backpack, its not going to make a difference in your ability to find that person. It's not going to be worth the time to take off your pack and dig through it to find your phone and turn it off before doing a proper search.

Final thoughts, there is a rather substantial difference in the accuracy and range of the Tracker 2 vs the Tracker 1, and once again between the Tracker 3 and 2. Honestly, if you were looking for a reason to upgrade transceivers go to your local shop and have your buddies all get together and go play in a park this summer and you will quickly learn that there is a substantial difference between units.

It's good to know that you've thought about it and even tested it yourself. I haven't tried it out with my newer beacon (an Arva Neo), but I did test it out years ago with buddies and their Pieps DSPs. The interference definitely made the locking on take longer as the direction swung about.
Talking about older transceivers though, when we were testing it out I was using an old F1 and had no issue with interference. I figured that spikes were more important than interference in the end though, so I did upgrade. I do miss the beeps though.

Generally when I travel in avalanche terrain I turn off all of my electronics before heading into the backcountry. That way I don't have to worry about this interference if I do ever need to use my beacon.

I think its good to share perspectives like this, and experiences with the community. Now if we can just get the slednecks to start to wear their transceivers instead of putting them in their backpacks on their sleds we could avoid a lot more deaths every year.
